Depth is cubed and timber buys it cheaply: a 2x6 is of order twice as stiff as a 2550, and a 4x4 about seven times a 2525 and better in buckling. Timber also damps, where aluminium rings. Extrusion's one real advantage over timber here is dimensional stability - and that is precisely what the three-point mount above already solves, which is why it is not a reason to spend the extrusion on the base. Spend it on the machine's own structure, where spans are short and the rails locate off it.

## [linear-encoder/controller-board.md](linear-encoder/controller-board.md)  (1)

- OPEN: [L12](linear-encoder/controller-board.md#the-jacks-must-not-have-integrated-magnetics) — *Controller board (daughter board)*<br>The jacks must NOT have integrated magnetics Most 4-port RJ45 assemblies sold for Ethernet are MagJacks - transformers inside. Transformers block DC, and every signal here is DC-coupled: A, B, MagDECn and the 3.3 V feed. With magnetics fitted nothing works at all - not degraded, dead - and it costs a board spin to discover.

It is recorded because the reasoning is long, several blind alleys were walked and closed on the way, and the alternative is re-walking them. The tape-mounting text above assumes the tape lies directly on the 45 mm front strip, which is what this would change.
- FLAG: [L262](linear-encoder/design-can-position-feedback.md#proposal---a-printed-carrier-to-lift-the-tape-clear-of-the-bolt-heads) — *1.4 Physical layout / PROPOSAL - a printed carrier to lift…*<br>Why the bond to the aluminium is the whole design, and why plastic was nearly wrong. §1.4's standing rule is bond the full length so the band is dragged by its substrate and the scale tracks the machine's real thermal growth — with an explicit "do not improve it into a one-end anchor later". That rule works because the substrate overwhelms the band: the 45 × 4 aluminium strip is of order 12,000 kN axially against a 15 × 4 printed carrier's ~180 kN. Aluminium commands the steel band. A printed strip commands nothing, and if it is left floating — located only by the bolt heads — then the tape's own steel band becomes the stiff member and the assembly reports steel's 11.7 µm/m/K while the machine moves on aluminium's 23.1. That is precisely the failure the full-length bond exists to prevent, arrived at from a different direction, and segmenting makes it worse rather than better.
- OPEN: [L378](linear-encoder/design-can-position-feedback.md#the-sensor-mount-a-clamped-puck-in-a-35-mm-bore) — *1.4 Physical layout / The sensor mount: a clamped puck in a…*<br>WHICH WAY THE TAPE FACES ON X, Y1 AND Y2 IS NOT DECIDED - only Z is. Z was confirmed vertical, so debris falls off it. The other three are each a metre of exposed magnet, and facing one of them upward is a metre of surface collecting dust for the life of the machine. The rule above says prefer down or inward; this is the note that it has not actually been applied to three of the four axes. Decide it before the tape is cut, because the tape is one-shot PSA and the bracket design follows from the face.
- FLAG: [L613](linear-encoder/design-can-position-feedback.md#the-core-does-have-a-can-layer-and-it-is-scaffolding) — *7. grblHAL integration / The core DOES have a CAN layer — a…*<br>THE PUMP IS task_add_systick: EVERY 1 ms, ONE TX AND ONE RX MESSAGE PER TICK. That is a hard ceiling of 1000 frames per second each way regardless of bus rate, with RX callback latency of up to 1 ms after the ISR queued it. The ring buffers are 8 deep. This is the single most important fact about the layer, because it is a software ceiling that no amount of bus bandwidth relieves.
- OPEN: [L623](linear-encoder/design-can-position-feedback.md#the-core-does-have-a-can-layer-and-it-is-scaffolding) — *7. grblHAL integration / The core DOES have a CAN layer — a…*<br>NOBODY USES IT. The only consumer in the tree is report.c calling canbus_enabled() to append "CAN," to the $I options string. And the Teensy / iMXRT1062 driver implements none of the hooks — only the copied weak stubs, and CANBUS_ENABLE is not offered in my_machine.h. On a Teensy 4.1 today CAN is a no-op: can_start returns false and the systick task never registers.

- FLAG: [L47](commissioning/masses.md#why-these-were-weighed) — *Measured masses / Why these were weighed*<br>Reflected inertia is why the gantry's mass nearly vanishes from the motor decision, and these are the numbers that showed it. Through a 5 mm lead, load mass reaches the motor shaft as mass x (lead / 2π)² - and ../machine/stepper-sizing.md works that to 6.3 x 10⁻⁷ kg·m² per kilogram, which puts the whole 58 kg below the screw's own inertia. So these masses settle the structural questions - what the risers carry, what the three-point mount carries, what has to be lifted - and are very nearly irrelevant to motor sizing. Reading them the other way round is the mistake they invite.

## [wiring/cabinet-power-and-grounding.md](wiring/cabinet-power-and-grounding.md)  (5)

- FLAG: [L33](wiring/cabinet-power-and-grounding.md#the-motor-supply-is-not-settled) — *Cabinet power and grounding / The motor supply is not settl…*<br>NAMEPLATE, NOT MEASURED. This is the supply's own claim about itself.
- FLAG: [L106](wiring/cabinet-power-and-grounding.md#separate-the-logic-supply-from-the-motor-rail) — *Cabinet power and grounding / Separate the logic supply fro…*<br>CHECK THE 5 V REGULATOR'S ABSOLUTE MAXIMUM INPUT BEFORE TRUSTING ANY OF THIS, AND SIZE IT ON WHAT THE RAIL CAN REACH RATHER THAN ON ITS NOMINAL 36 V. The ceiling is whatever the drives tolerate before they trip, and the TST57 manual puts the drives' over-voltage alarm above 50 V - see ig57-drives.md, where the rail voltage is now the largest open decision. A regulator chosen with no margin dies taking the controller with it, mid-job, which is the failure that looks like a random crash and gets diagnosed as firmware. This paragraph said 55 V until 2026-10-12, from the Mega V's drives; do not reinstate that figure.
- FLAG: [L114](wiring/cabinet-power-and-grounding.md#separate-the-logic-supply-from-the-motor-rail) — *Cabinet power and grounding / Separate the logic supply fro…*<br>THE ISOLATION IS THERE, AND IT IS EASY TO SHORT OUT BY ACCIDENT. The IG57 brings its control signals out as plus/minus pairs - PU+/PU-, DR+/DR-, EN+/EN-, AL+/AL- - which is an opto input presented at its two ends, so the galvanic isolation is real. The four minus legs are commoned inside the drive on the seller's word, so it is one isolated common per drive rather than four isolated signals; the boundary that matters, between each drive and the controller, is the one that exists. See ig57-drives.md, where the meter check that confirms it is written down.
- FLAG: [L139](wiring/cabinet-power-and-grounding.md#grounds-meet-at-one-pe-bus-bar) — *Cabinet power and grounding / Grounds meet at one PE bus bar*<br>NOT AT THE 240 V INPUT, AND NEVER THROUGH A SIGNAL WIRE. The supplies are isolated, so the mains input is not a ground reference for the DC side. And a ground that arrives through a signal conductor is a ground that carries signal current - which is the same mistake as the daisy-chained motor returns in breakout-box.md, one level up.
- FLAG: [L177](wiring/cabinet-power-and-grounding.md#the-mains-circuit) — *Cabinet power and grounding / The mains circuit*<br>PUT THE VFD ON ITS OWN BRANCH REGARDLESS, and an EMI filter or line reactor on its input. VFDs are electrically filthy. This is the same principle as keeping the ESP32 off the probe rail, at mains scale - and the reason to do it even when the arithmetic says one circuit carries the load is that the arithmetic is about current, not about noise.
